# The Image Problem {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Images Are Big {.center}

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Width × Height | 224 × 224 pixels |
| Colour channels | 3 (red, green, blue) |
| Total numbers | **150,528** |
| Weights in first layer (256 neurons) | ~38 million |

- A standard fully connected network applied to images would have an enormous number of weights
- Most of those weights would learn nothing useful, there is too much to learn from too little signal

::: notes
- A 224×224 colour image is over 150,000 numbers
- A single fully connected layer with 256 neurons would have ~38 million weights
- Training those weights reliably requires an enormous amount of data
- A standard network cannot exploit the fact that an edge at (100,100) is similar to one at (101,100)
:::

## No Sense of Space

:::: {.nn-layout}
```{mermaid}
graph LR
  p1["pixel at 100,100"] --> N["neuron"]
  p2["pixel at 100,101"] --> N
  p3["pixel at 200,100"] --> N
  p4["pixel at 224,224"] --> N
```
::: {.nn-bullets}
- A fully connected network treats every pixel as equally related to every other pixel
- But nearby pixels carry related information, distant pixels do not
- Images have **spatial structure** that standard networks are blind to
:::
::::

::: notes
- Fully connected networks receive every pixel with no information about which are neighbours
- Images are not collections of independent numbers, they are spatially structured
- A network that exploits spatial structure learns far more efficiently from far less data
- CNNs are designed to do exactly this
:::

# Convolution {background-color="#1a252f"}

## A Sliding Window {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  img["Image: 224 x 224"] --> conv["Filter slides<br/>across image: 3 x 3"] --> fm["Feature Map:<br/>where is the pattern?"]
```

- A **filter** (also called a kernel) is a small grid of weights (e.g. 3x3)
- It slides across every position in the image
- At each position, multiply the overlapping pixels by the filter weights, sum them up
- The result is a **feature map** showing where the pattern was detected

::: notes
- Instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron, a small filter (e.g. 3×3) slides across the image
- At each position, compute a weighted sum of the overlapping pixels
- Output is a feature map, each value shows how strongly the pattern appeared at that position
- One filter produces one feature map; a layer applies 32, 64, or 128 filters simultaneously
:::

## One Filter, One Pattern {.center}

| Filter | What it detects | Feature map shows |
|--------|----------------|-------------------|
| Filter A | Horizontal edges | Horizontal boundaries in the image |
| Filter B | Vertical edges | Vertical boundaries |
| Filter C | Bright spots | Regions of high local brightness |

- Each filter learns to detect **one specific pattern**
- A layer with 64 filters produces 64 feature maps — 64 different "views" of the image
- The network learns **which filters are useful** during training

::: notes
- Filters are not hand-designed, the network learns them from data
- Before training — Random; after training: detect patterns useful for the task (vessel edges, brightness gradients)
- The number of filters per layer is a design choice — more filters, more patterns detected, more computation
:::

# What Filters Learn {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Simple to Complex {.center}

- We saw this feature hierarchy in the previous session. Convolution is the mechanism that produces it.

| Layer depth | Typical features detected |
|-------------|--------------------------|
| Layer 1 | Edges, colour gradients, brightness changes |
| Layer 2 | Corners, curves, short line segments |
| Layer 3 | Textures, shapes, repeating patterns |
| Layer 4+ | Complex structures, object parts, semantic features |

- Each layer builds on the feature maps of the layer before it
- Complexity increases with depth automatically, through training

::: notes
- The hierarchy is not programmed, it emerges as the most efficient way to represent the data
- Early layers — Low-level features (edges, gradients, colour transitions)
- Middle layers — More complex patterns (shapes, textures)
- Late layers — High-level, semantically meaningful features
- For retinal images — Early = vessel edges; middle = vessel branching; late = global disease indicators
:::

## What a Trained Network Detects {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph TD
  A["Blood vessel edges<br/>(early layers)"] --> B["Vessel branching<br/>patterns"]
  C["Lesion boundaries<br/>(early layers)"] --> D["Lesion shape<br/>and density"]
  B --> E["Global disease<br/>indicators (late layers)"]
  D --> E
  E --> F["Disease / No disease"]
```

::: notes
- This diagram is approximate, the network discovers this structure; we cannot fully interpret every neuron
- Broad pattern: early features are local and simple, late features are global and complex
- Tools like Grad-CAM can visualise which parts of a retinal image the network focuses on
- Typically, optic disc, vessel branching points, and regions with visible lesions
:::

# Pooling {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Downsampling the Feature Map {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  fm["Feature Map: 224 x 224"] --> pool["Max Pooling:<br/>2x2, stride 2"] --> small["Smaller Map: 112 x 112"]
```

- **Max pooling** — Divide the feature map into small regions, keep the maximum value from each
- Halves the spatial dimensions with a 2×2 pool, stride 2
- Keeps the strongest signal, discards fine spatial detail

::: notes
- Max pooling — Divide the feature map into 2×2 regions, keep only the maximum value from each
- Result — Feature map half the width and height of the input
- Reduces computation in subsequent layers and retains only the most salient features
- Applied after each conv layer — Spatial dimensions shrink, number of channels grows
:::

## Small Shifts Do Not Matter {.center}

- If the pattern moves a few pixels, the max-pooled value stays roughly the same
- The network does not need to see the same pattern in exactly the same location to recognise it
- This is called **translation invariance**, it is critical for real-world images

> A blood vessel does not need to be centred in the image to be detected.

::: notes
- In real datasets, the same structure appears at different positions across images
- Without pooling: the network would need separate detectors for every possible position
- Pooling generalises across positions, if the pattern appeared anywhere in the 2×2 region, it is preserved
- A blood vessel at any position in a retinal image will still be detected
:::

# CNN Architecture {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Stacking Convolutional Blocks {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  img["Input<br/>224×224×3"] --> b1["Conv Block 1<br/>→ 112×112"] --> b2["Block 2<br/>→ 56×56"] --> b3["Block 3<br/>→ 28×28"] --> b4["Block 4<br/>→ 14×14"] --> head["FC Head<br/>Classification"]
```

- Each block — Convolution → Activation (ReLU) → Max Pooling
- Spatial dimensions **shrink** with each block
- Number of channels (filters) **grows**: 3 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256

::: notes
- Standard block: Conv → ReLU → Max Pooling, stacked repeatedly
- Each block halves spatial dimensions and deepens the channel dimension
- After 4 blocks: 14×14 spatial, 256 channels, each representing a complex pattern
- A fully connected head then converts the feature maps to a class prediction
:::

## The Baseline CNN in This Project {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["Input<br/>224×224, 3ch"] --> B["Conv Blocks ×4<br/>32→64→128→256ch"] --> C["AvgPool<br/>1×1, 256-dim"] --> D["FC Head<br/>256→128→2"] --> E["Disease /<br/>No disease"]
```

- Four convolutional blocks, each building on the features of the last
- Adaptive average pooling collapses spatial dimensions regardless of input size
- Two fully connected layers with dropout for regularisation

::: notes
- Each block follows Conv2d → BatchNorm2d → ReLU → MaxPool2d
- Channels grow: 3 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256
- Adaptive average pooling always produces a 256-dim feature vector regardless of input size
- FC head maps to two output scores: healthy vs disease
:::

# The Retinopathy Context {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Why CNNs Are a Natural Fit {.center}

| Property | Why it matters for retinal images |
|----------|----------------------------------|
| Spatial structure | Vessel patterns and lesions are spatially localised |
| Translation invariance | Disease indicators appear anywhere in the image |
| Feature hierarchy | From vessel edges to global disease patterns |
| Parameter efficiency | ~5,700 training images, far fewer than needed for fully connected |

::: notes
- Fundus images have clear spatial structure: circular optic disc, radial vessels, localised lesions
- CNNs are designed to exploit exactly this kind of structure
- Translation invariance handles variation in field-of-view and image alignment across datasets
- With only ~5,700 training images, CNN parameter efficiency is not a luxury, it is a necessity
:::

# Transfer Learning {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Standing on the Shoulders of Giants {.center}

| | ImageNet training | Fine-tuning for retinopathy |
|--|--|--|
| Images | 1.2 million | ~5,700 |
| Categories | 1,000 | 2 |
| Training time | Weeks (on specialist hardware) | Hours (on a laptop) |
| What is learned | Rich general visual features | Task-specific adaptations |

- We **start** with a network already trained on ImageNet
- Its weights already encode a sophisticated understanding of visual patterns
- We then **adapt** those weights to our specific task

::: notes
- Training a network from scratch on ImageNet takes weeks on specialist hardware
- The pre-trained weights encode rich, general-purpose visual features useful for many tasks
- Instead of repeating this for every task, we start with pre-trained weights and adapt them
- With ~5,700 images, this is not just convenient, it is often the only practical path to a good model
:::

## Pre-Trained Weights Encode General Vision {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  imagenet["1.2M ImageNet images<br/>1,000 categories"] --> pretrained["Pre-trained<br/>ResNet-18"] --> finetune["Fine-tuning on<br/>retinal images"] --> classifier["Retinopathy<br/>classifier"]
```

- ResNet-18 — 18-layer deep network, pre-trained on ImageNet
- We replace only the final layer (1,000 categories → 2 categories)
- Everything else—17 layers of learned visual features—is kept and adapted

::: notes
- ResNet-18 — 18-layer network with residual connections (shortcuts that stabilise training of deep networks)
- Pre-trained on ImageNet; we replace only the final classification layer (1,000 → 2 categories)
- The rest of the network—17 layers of learned visual features—is kept and adapted, not discarded
:::

# Why Fine-Tuning Works {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Universal vs Task-Specific Features {.center}

| Location | What is learned | Strategy |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| Early layers | Edges, curves, textures — universal | **Keep** — these transfer to any vision task |
| Middle layers | Shapes, patterns — partially universal | **Lightly adapt** |
| Late layers | Task-specific, high-level features | **Fully retrain** — adapt to retinopathy |

::: notes
- Early layer features (edges, curves, textures) appear in retinal images just as in photographs of cats and cars
- Discarding and relearning these from scratch would be wasteful
- Late layers encode ImageNet-specific features (cars, dogs, birds) (less useful for retinopathy)
- Strategy — Keep early layers, retrain late layers guided by retinal image data
:::

## The Two-Phase Fine-Tuning Strategy {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["Pre-trained ResNet-18<br/>(backbone frozen)"] -->|"Phase 1: 5 epochs, lr = 1e-3"| B["Head stabilises,<br/>backbone unchanged"] -->|"Phase 2: ≤30 epochs, lr = 1e-4"| C["All layers<br/>fine-tuned"]
```

- **Phase 1** — Train only the new classification head — the backbone is frozen
- **Phase 2** — Unfreeze everything and train the whole network at a lower learning rate
- You will see exactly this two-phase pattern in the code during Session 4

::: notes
- Unfreezing everything immediately risks large, noisy gradients from the random head corrupting pre-trained weights
- Phase 1: train only the head — let it stabilise before it influences the backbone
- Phase 2: unfreeze everything, train at a much lower learning rate — nudge rather than overwrite
- This is the exact approach used in the notebook
:::

# Key Takeaways {background-color="#1a252f"}

## The Bigger Picture {.center}

- A CNN doesn't look at every pixel at once — a small filter slides across the image, detecting one pattern at a time, which is why CNNs work so well with limited data.
- The feature hierarchy — edges, then shapes, then structures — isn't programmed in; it emerges because that's the most efficient way to represent the data.
- Weights trained on photographs of cats and dogs already encode a sophisticated understanding of visual structure; adapting them to retinal images takes hours, not weeks.
